title: Sudden severe occipital headache at the gym
presenting_complaint: Sudden, severe occipital headache that developed 2 hours ago while at the gym and peaked within a minute — "like being hit with a bat". She vomited twice.
history: 48-year-old female teacher. No loss of consciousness, no seizure, no head trauma. Past medical history: hypertension, poorly controlled, on amlodipine. Smokes. Mother died of a "brain bleed" at 52. Not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

findings.name: Neurological examination
findings.value: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no focal neurological deficit

findings.name: Meningeal signs
findings.value: photophobia present, neck stiffness present, Kernig sign negative

findings.name: Non-contrast head CT (2 hours from onset)
findings.value: hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and the Sylvian fissures

findings.name: CT angiography
findings.value: 7 mm aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery

diagnosis_options.label: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
diagnosis_options.explanation: Thunderclap occipital headache peaking within a minute, vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness, with hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures on non-contrast CT and a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CT angiography. Family history of "brain bleed" and smoking are additional risk factors.

diagnosis_options.label: Migraine
diagnosis_options.explanation: Migraine does not typically present with a thunderclap headache peaking within one minute, meningism and subarachnoid blood on CT.

diagnosis_options.label: Bacterial meningitis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Fever is minimal (37.4 °C) and the CT shows subarachnoid blood with an aneurysm; the presentation is not that of bacterial meningitis.

diagnosis_options.label: Hypertensive encephalopathy
diagnosis_options.explanation: Blood pressure is elevated, but there is no encephalopathy (GCS 15, no focal deficit) and the CT findings are those of subarachnoid haemorrhage.

diagnosis_options.label: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
diagnosis_options.explanation: RCVS can cause thunderclap headache, but CT shows subarachnoid blood and CT angiography demonstrates a saccular aneurysm, not the diffuse segmental vasoconstriction typical of RCVS.

management_options.label: Urgent neurosurgical / neurointerventional referral for aneurysm securing (coiling or clipping)
management_options.explanation: Essential: the aneurysm must be secured urgently to prevent rebleeding.

management_options.label: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours
management_options.explanation: Essential: nimodipine improves outcome by reducing delayed cerebral ischaemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

management_options.label: Control systolic BP below 160 mmHg with a titratable IV agent
management_options.explanation: Essential: blood pressure control reduces the risk of rebleeding from the unsecured aneurysm.

management_options.label: Analgesia and antiemetic
management_options.explanation: Reasonable supportive measure for headache and vomiting.

management_options.label: Lumbar puncture now
management_options.explanation: Harmful: not needed after a diagnostic CT showing subarachnoid blood, and it risks rebleeding.

management_options.label: Aspirin
management_options.explanation: Harmful in an unsecured aneurysm: antiplatelet therapy increases the risk of rebleeding.
